en: The Eight Vowels of Śikṣā, Śrī Hari: Om!

The junction between the end of one word and the beginning of another—when there is a single vital breath (*prāṇa*) connecting the end of the preceding word and the beginning of the following word—that is designated as *sandhi*. A later [operation] does not apply when an earlier [operation] has already occurred. Furthermore, when an earlier *sandhi* rule is prescribed, a later *sandhi* rule does not take effect. Example 1: *a āmapare* (When *a* is followed by *ā*, it becomes *ā*). Example 2: *tava ayam* → *tavāyam*.
The vowel *e* [is substituted] for *i* and *ī*: *tava idam* becomes *tavedam*.
(3) The vowel *o* [is substituted] for *u* and *ū*: *tava uruḥ* becomes *tavoruḥ*.
(4) *ā* [is substituted] for *ṛ* and *ṝ*: *svāhā ṛṣabham* becomes *svāhārṣabham*. (5)

The vowel *ai* [is substituted] when followed by *ai*: *tava etat* becomes *tavaitat*; *tava aiśvaryam* becomes *tavaiśvaryam*. The vowel *au* [is substituted] when followed by *au*: *tava ojaḥ* becomes *tavaujaḥ*.
*pra’aukṣan*, *praukṣan* (7); before a vowel, *iryyam* becomes *vājī’arvan*, *vvājjyarvan*; *vi’ūrṇum ṣe*, *vyūrṇuṃṣe*; *asi’ṛtasya*, *asyṛtasya* (8);
before the letter *i*, *irim* becomes *vīta*, *vvīta* (9).
The letter *u* [is elided] before a vowel: *nu indra*, *nu indra*;
*uru u varṇe*, *anu ut*, *anu ut*. The letter *ṛ* [becomes] *r* before a vowel: *dhātṛ aṃśaḥ*, *dhātr aṃśaḥ*.
An *ṛ*-vowel [remains unchanged] before an *ṛ*-vowel or an *ṛ*-vowel. *hotṛ-ṛkāraḥ* becomes *hotṛkāraḥ*. (13) This *e*-vowel [remains unchanged] before a vowel. *agne-āyāhi* becomes *agna āyāhi*.
(14) This *o*-vowel becomes *avaṃ* before a vowel. *viṣṇo-ete* becomes *viṣṇavete*. (15)

Among those, the first characteristic is as follows: *e* and *ai* undergo elision (*lopa*). As in *te 'vantu* [becoming] *tevantu*; *vo lopaṃ o-au-ṣu* [becoming] *ubhau u* [and] *ubhā u*. Why say "in *o*, *au*, and *ṣu*"? [Because otherwise, as in] *palakyā-v-aho-rātre*, there would be an endless vowel-sandhi (*ac-sandhi*) produced by the suffix *kṛt*.

Now begins the section on accents (*svaraprakaraṇa*). The accents are the acute (*udātta*), the grave (*anudātta*), the circumflex (*svarita*), and the protracted (*pracaya*). 1. The acute (*udātta*) is marked by a red line above; for example: *śam*, *pra*, *nu*, or the second [syllable] of a word. For example: *adho rakto'nudāttaḥ* (the grave is marked with a red line below). For example: *rudra'īḍe*. 2. The grave (*anudātta*) is marked by a red line below; for example: *rudra'īḍe*. 3. The circumflex (*svarita*) is marked by a dot above; for example: *śam*. 4. The protracted (*pracaya*) is marked by a dot below; for example: *pra*. 5. When there is no mark, it is understood to be grave (*anudātta*); for example: *nu*. 6. A syllable following an acute (*udātta*) is circumflex (*svarita*); for example: *dvitīyasya*. 7. A syllable following a circumflex (*svarita*) is grave (*anudātta*); for example: *adho rakto'nudāttaḥ*. 8. A syllable following a grave (*anudātta*) is protracted (*pracaya*); for example: *rudra'īḍe*. 9. The end of a sentence is always acute (*udātta*); for example: *śam*. 10. The beginning of a sentence is always grave (*anudātta*); for example: *pra*. 11. A syllable that is part of a compound is always grave (*anudātta*); for example: *nu*. 12. A syllable that is not part of a compound is always acute (*udātta*); for example: *dvitīyasya*. 13. A syllable that is both part of a compound and follows another compound is always circumflex (*svarita*); for example: *adho rakto'nudāttaḥ*. 14. A syllable that is neither part of a compound nor follows another compound is always grave (*anudātta*); for example: *rudra'īḍe*.
And as for the third [type]: a *svarita* is marked with a red stroke above or a red stroke across, as in *svaḥ*, *svaḥ*, *svaḥ* (4).
Those that are downward-turned (*nyubja*), followed by a red stroke, are *udātta*, as in *svāhā* and *svarṇārkaḥ* (5).
And as for the fourth [type]: those that follow a *svarita* and have a downward-turned red stroke are *pracaya*, as in *tryambakaṃ yajāmahe* (6).

The *svarita* is of five kinds, distinguished as *jātya*, *abhinihita*, *kṣaipra*, *praśliṣṭa*, and [the others]. 1. *Jātya*: When, within a single word, a low-pitched (*anudātta*) vowel is followed by either a *y* or a *v*, it becomes *jātya*. Example: *dhānyam*; *svaḥ*. 2. *Abhinihita*: When an *udātta* vowel is substituted for an *e* or *o* due to the elision of the vowel *a*, the resulting *svarita* is *abhinihita*. Examples: *te 'vantu* (from *te avantu*); *vedo 'si* (from *vedo asi*). 3. *Kṣaipra*: When a low-pitched (*anudātta*) vowel follows a *y* or a *v* in place of an *udātta* vowel *i*, it is *kṣaipra*. Examples: *yu yoddhayasmat*; *nu indra* (from *nu indra*).
The vowel *i* is a coalescence (*praśliṣṭa*) in place of a short *udātta* and a short *anudātta*.

*vi'ita*, *vvīta* (10)—the four beginning with *anudāttapūrvajāti* and so on, like the gift to the father, are in the hand. *vāyavyaiḥ*. *bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. *te 'vantu*. *vedo'si*. *abhyabhi*. *yojānvindra*.
*divīva* (11)—the four beginning with *anudāttapūrvajāti* and so on, like the gift to a human, are in the raised tone (*udātta*).

So am I. That which is the intermediate space—this world is well-supported, firmly established; heaven is well-supported. (13) [The four rules beginning with] *anudāttapūrva* and *jāti*, etc., apply at the root of the ear (*karṇamūla*) when there is an absence of a following acute (*udātta*) or circumflex (*svarita*) accent. *nyaṅ*. *svaḥ*. *te'vantu*. *so'smi*. *tryambakam nvindra*. *vvīta*. (14)

An unaccented vowel following an acute accent becomes circumflex (*svarita*). This does not occur when followed by an acute or circumflex accent, as in *iṣe tvā* (15) and *ūrje tvā*. Also, it does not occur in *īśā vasyam*. Following a circumflex accent, there is a monotone (*pracaya*) for the subsequent unaccented vowels, as in *vāyava stha* (16).

There is no [change] when followed by an acute (udātta) or a circumflex (svarita) accent. *vāyava stha devāḥ*; *vāsyamidam*. For an acute [vowel] following an acute is indeed [regarded as] acute. *pra'rpa yatu*; *prārppayatu*. After an acute, there occurs the enclitic circumflex (*nihatasvāra*); after a circumflex, there occurs the protracted (*pracaya*). No other accent occurs before an acute or a circumflex. 19. 3.

Thus, Fortune (Lakṣmī) abandons even the wielder of the discus (Viṣṇu) if he wears tattered clothes, bears the stains of his teeth, eats excessively, speaks harshly, and sleeps at sunrise and sunset— this is the "Goad for the Self" (Svarāṅkuśa). 1.4.14.

Now, the characteristics of the placement of the hands: the *anudātta* (low-pitched) is to be known as being at the heart; the *udātta* (high-pitched) is declared to be at the head; the *svarita* (circumflex) should be at the root of the ear; and the *pracaya* (continuous) is remembered as being at the tip of the nose.

For "iṣe tvā" and "vāyava stha," one should begin from the left eyebrow when moving from an *udātta* to an *anudātta*. For "iṣe tvā" and "ūrje tvā," one should place [the hand] sequentially on the right side when moving from an *udātta* to a *svarita*.
*iṣe tvā*. 3. 5.

In the fifth [section]: *kaṭatapā*, *ṅaṇanamāḥ*; *vvāk manaḥ*, *vāṅmanaḥ*; *vvaṭmahān*, *vvaṇmahān*; *tat mitrasya*, *tanmitrasya*; *anuṣṭummātyā*. 2.

The *ja* sounds [become *ya*] after those [nasals], and the *śa*-class sounds [become *cha*]; that is the *citram*. That is the *citram*. Enjoy that; enjoy that. [In the word] *ādityān śmaśrubhiḥ*, there is *laṃlle*. [In] *paricit*, [there is] *lokaṃ*.

[In] *paricillokam*, there is *laṃlle* when followed by a nasal. Those worlds; those worlds. When followed by a short vowel, there is doubling in the *nau* (the *n* and *u* sounds). *Dadhyaṅ* the seer; *dadhyaṅṅṛṣiḥ*. *Aśman*. *Ūrjam*.

Before *naḥ* followed by *śa* or *cha*, the preceding [nasal] becomes an anusvāra; as in *ahīn* and *ahīm̐śca*. (7) Before *sa* and *ta* followed by *tha*, the preceding [nasal] becomes an anusvāra; as in *tān* and *tvam*, [becoming] *tāṃstvaṃ*.
(8) Before *maḥ* followed by a stop (*sparśa*), the following fifth letter [of its own class] is substituted; as in *vrataṅkṛṇata* and *vratañcariṣyāmi*, and *apāmphenena*. (9)

Before the letter *s*, [the augment] *k* occurs after *ṅ* and *t*. Before the letter *s*, the augments *kāgama* and *tāgama* are applied. *prāṅsomaḥ* / *prāṅksomaḥ*; *trīn samudrān* / *trīntsamudrān*.

Before nasalized (*anunāsika*) *y*, *v*, and *l*, as well as before non-nasalized *y*, *v*, and *l*, [the final *m* is replaced by *anusvāra*]. *sam yaumi* / *saṃyyaumi*; *tam vvaḥ* / *taṃvvaḥ*; *tam lokam* / *taṃlokam*.
Before *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, *h*, and *r*, [the final *m* is replaced by] the vowel *aṃ*. *saṃ śivam*; *havīṃṣyā*; *saṃ śiśādhi*; *saṃsaḥ*; *apāṃ retāṃsi*.
A *cha* or *śa* following a *jha*-class consonant [is doubled]. For example: *tac-chukram* (that pure), *tac-chukram*. 13.

A *ha* following a *jha*-class consonant becomes the fourth [consonant of its own class]. For example: *bhiṣak-homaḥ* (the physician’s oblation) becomes *bhiṣag-ghomaḥ*; *tat-haviḥ* (that oblation-material) becomes *tad-dhaviḥ*; *samrāṭ-homaḥ* (the sovereign’s oblation) becomes *sammrāḍ-ḍhomaḥ*. 14.
When preceded by a vowel, the first member of a conjunct consonant is doubled. For example: *iṣe tvā* (for food, thee) becomes *iṣe ttvā*. 15.
[The consonant] following *ra* and *ha* [is doubled]. *Sūryyam*, *bāhyam*. 16.
A *sparśa* [stop] following a sibilant (*ūṣman*) or a semi-vowel (*antasthā*) [is doubled]. *Vvāyavastha*. *Vvāyavastha*. 17. 6. 4. Thus ends the *hal-sandhi* (consonant-sandhi) composed by Ananta.

The second *visarga* [is elided] before *u* and *aś*. Examples: *śivaḥ asi* becomes *śivo'si*; *devebhyaḥ haviḥ* becomes *devebhyo haviḥ*. 1. Regarding the elision of the final [visarga] when it follows another [word]: *devāḥ atra* becomes *devā'tra*; *devāḥ āśāḥ* becomes *devā'āśāḥ*. 2. [Note: This rule applies when the preceding word ends in *a* or *ā*.]
Another [instance of] elision occurs before a *parasmaipada* suffix: *devaḥ* + *āśāḥ* → *devāśāḥ*. Another [instance of] elision occurs before a *haś* (consonant) suffix:
*devāḥ* + *hasanti* → *devā hasanti*. Another [instance of] elision occurs before an *ic* (vowel) suffix: *devāḥ* + *iha* → *devā iha*.

*agvnyāḥ* | *indrāya* | *agdha nyā' indrāya* (5) — when there is *repha* (the letter *r*) and *icyara* (the vowel *i*), the *repha* is elided; as in *savitaḥ' jajāna* | *savitarrjajāna*. *agniḥ' ekākṣareṇa* | *agnirekākṣareṇa* (6) — when there is *repha* followed by *ecyara* (vowels *e* or *o*), there is elision of the *repha*, and the preceding [vowel] becomes long; as in *prātaḥ'rātriḥ* | *prātā rātriḥ*. *ruruḥ raudraḥ* | *rurū raudraḥ* (7) — [The same rule applies].
The visarga of *eṣaḥ* and *syaḥ* is elided before a consonant. *eṣaḥ syaḥ* becomes *eṣa syaḥ*. *syaḥ*. *rātthyaḥ*. *sya rātthyaḥ*. *saḥ*. *naḥ*. *sa naḥ*.
*saḥ te*. *saste*. *namaḥ te*. *namaste*.

When followed by *cha* or *para*, there is *śam*. Also when followed by *vāja*. [The rule] "and *vāja*" [is repeated]. 10. *lopaṃ kharpare śari*: [The visarga] is elided before a sibilant (*śar*) followed by a hard consonant (*kharpar*). *andhaḥ stha* becomes *andha sttha*. 11. 7.5. Thus ends the section on the euphonic combination of the visarga (*visargasandhiḥ*).
